stem: A patient on long-term metformin and a PPI has numb feet and macrocytic anemia. What should be checked?
why_correct: Long-term PPI and metformin use impair B12 (less acid release; impaired ileal uptake); deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neuropathy.
takeaway: Monitor B12 in long-term PPI or metformin users.
discriminator: Iron deficiency → microcytic; B12/folate → megaloblastic.

D.why: Long-term PPI and metformin use impair B12 (less acid release; impaired ileal uptake); deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neuropathy.

stem: A patient takes omeprazole at bedtime with no benefit. What counseling best improves its effect?
correct: Take it 30–60 minutes before the first meal

distractors.text: Take it with a calcium tablet at night
Crush the tablet and take it with milk
Double the dose and keep bedtime timing

distractors.why: PPIs work on active pumps daily.

why_correct: PPIs work best on actively secreting pumps; dosing 30–60 minutes before the first meal matches peak pump activity.
takeaway: PPI before breakfast; H2 blocker is the bedtime/nocturnal drug.
discriminator: PPIs need active pumps; antacids don’t.

A.text: Take it 30–60 minutes before the first meal
A.why: PPIs work best on actively secreting pumps; dosing 30–60 minutes before the first meal matches peak pump activity.

B.text: Crush the tablet and take it with milk

C.text: Double the dose and keep bedtime timing

D.why: PPIs work on active pumps daily.

E.text: Take it with a calcium tablet at night

stem: A patient with moderate-to-severe Crohn disease is about to start infliximab. Which pre-treatment step is required?
correct: Screen for TB and hepatitis B/C; update vaccines

distractors.text: Give a live vaccine after the first dose

distractors.why: Biologics reactivate TB and hepatitis B.

why_correct: Before biologics: TB and hepatitis B/C screening, vaccines (especially live) updated first, then regular labs.
takeaway: Biologic risk = infection, across organ systems.
discriminator: Same framework as the RA biologics in Unit 2.

A.text: Screen for TB and hepatitis B/C; update vaccines
A.why: Before biologics: TB and hepatitis B/C screening, vaccines (especially live) updated first, then regular labs.

C.why: Biologics reactivate TB and hepatitis B.

D.text: Give a live vaccine after the first dose

stem: A patient stable on warfarin starts St. John’s wort for mood. What should the clinician anticipate?

distractors.text: No change, since it is natural
Higher INR from added vitamin K

why_correct: St. John’s wort induces CYP3A4, speeding warfarin metabolism and lowering INR; check INR when starting or stopping any supplement.
takeaway: Ask about supplements at every medication reconciliation.
discriminator: Vitamin K lowers INR pharmacodynamically; St. John’s wort pharmacokinetically.

C.why: St. John’s wort induces CYP3A4, speeding warfarin metabolism and lowering INR; check INR when starting or stopping any supplement.

D.text: No change, since it is natural

E.text: Higher INR from added vitamin K

stem: A patient with diabetic gastroparesis has taken metoclopramide for a year. What is the major safety concern?
why_correct: Metoclopramide’s boxed warning is tardive dyskinesia with prolonged use or high doses — avoid beyond 12 weeks.
takeaway: Limit metoclopramide to 12 weeks.
discriminator: Acute dystonia → diphenhydramine or benztropine.

B.why: Metoclopramide’s boxed warning is tardive dyskinesia with prolonged use or high doses — avoid beyond 12 weeks.

stem: A 28-year-old on daily naproxen for arthritis may become pregnant. Which ulcer-prevention drug is contraindicated?
why_correct: Misoprostol, a PGE1 analog used to prevent NSAID ulcers, is contraindicated in pregnancy — a potent uterotonic/abortifacient (boxed warning).
takeaway: Misoprostol: NSAID-ulcer prevention, never in pregnancy.
discriminator: Sucralfate = barrier; misoprostol = prostaglandin replacement.

D.why: Misoprostol, a PGE1 analog used to prevent NSAID ulcers, is contraindicated in pregnancy — a potent uterotonic/abortifacient (boxed warning).

stem: A patient with newly diagnosed mild ulcerative colitis is starting therapy. Which drug fits first?

distractors.why: Slow; maintenance, not first-line mild UC.

why_correct: 5-ASA agents are first-line for mild-to-moderate UC with a favorable safety profile; biologics are reserved for moderate-to-severe disease.
takeaway: Match therapy to severity (step therapy).
discriminator: Monitor mesalamine renal function.

A.why: Slow; maintenance, not first-line mild UC.

B.why: 5-ASA agents are first-line for mild-to-moderate UC with a favorable safety profile; biologics are reserved for moderate-to-severe disease.

stem: Why does diphenoxylate/atropine contain a low dose of atropine?
why_correct: Atropine is included at a subtherapeutic dose specifically to discourage misuse/overdose; the product is Schedule V.
takeaway: Lomotil: opioid + deterrent atropine.
discriminator: Loperamide stays out of the CNS via P-gp efflux.

E.why: Atropine is included at a subtherapeutic dose specifically to discourage misuse/overdose; the product is Schedule V.

stem: A patient with a new coronary stent on clopidogrel needs long-term GERD therapy. What should the clinician anticipate with omeprazole?
correct: Less clopidogrel activation via CYP2C19 inhibition

distractors.text: Excess bleeding from added antiplatelet effect
distractors.why: The effect is blunted, not enhanced.

distractors.text: No change, since both are cleared by the kidney

why_correct: Omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit CYP2C19, which activates the prodrug clopidogrel, potentially blunting its antiplatelet effect.
takeaway: Prodrug + inhibitor of its activating enzyme → therapeutic failure.
discriminator: Textbook: pantoprazole or rabeprazole preferred with clopidogrel.

B.text: Excess bleeding from added antiplatelet effect
B.why: The effect is blunted, not enhanced.

C.text: Less clopidogrel activation via CYP2C19 inhibition
C.why: Omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit CYP2C19, which activates the prodrug clopidogrel, potentially blunting its antiplatelet effect.

D.text: No change, since both are cleared by the kidney

stem: A patient in her first trimester has persistent nausea despite diet changes. Which is typically first-line?
why_correct: Pyridoxine, often combined with doxylamine, is typically first-line for nausea of pregnancy; ondansetron is used but first-trimester data are evolving.
takeaway: Pregnancy nausea → B6 ± doxylamine.
discriminator: Weigh maternal benefit against fetal risk.

E.why: Pyridoxine, often combined with doxylamine, is typically first-line for nausea of pregnancy; ondansetron is used but first-trimester data are evolving.

stem: Which laxative class has the slowest onset but is generally safest for long-term use?
why_correct: Bulk-forming agents absorb water and expand stool; slowest onset, safest long term; need fluids, avoid in obstruction.
takeaway: Relief tonight → osmotic or stimulant, not bulk-forming.
discriminator: PEG is first-line for chronic constipation.

B.why: Bulk-forming agents absorb water and expand stool; slowest onset, safest long term; need fluids, avoid in obstruction.

stem: A warfarin patient asks whether to stop eating leafy greens. What is the best counseling?
why_correct: Keep vitamin K intake consistent rather than avoiding it; INR is dosed against usual intake.
takeaway: Steady intake, steady INR.
discriminator: Ginkgo and fish oil raise bleeding risk.

B.why: Keep vitamin K intake consistent rather than avoiding it; INR is dosed against usual intake.

stem: Three days after clindamycin, a patient has profuse watery diarrhea and fever. Which plan is correct?
correct: Avoid loperamide; treat suspected C. difficile

distractors.why: Slows toxin clearance; toxic megacolon risk.
A laxative is not the treatment.

why_correct: This is concerning for C. difficile; avoid antimotility agents and treat with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin.
takeaway: Bloody, febrile, or post-antibiotic diarrhea → no antimotility agents.
discriminator: Clindamycin is the classic C. difficile antibiotic.

A.why: Slows toxin clearance; toxic megacolon risk.

C.text: Avoid loperamide; treat suspected C. difficile
C.why: This is concerning for C. difficile; avoid antimotility agents and treat with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin.

D.why: A laxative is not the treatment.

stem: Why should sucralfate be given on an empty stomach and apart from antacids or PPIs?
correct: It needs acid to polymerize and bind the ulcer base

distractors.text: It irreversibly blocks the proton pump

why_correct: Sucralfate polymerizes in acid (pH below 4) to form a protective barrier over the ulcer base; separate it from other drugs by 2 hours.
takeaway: Sucralfate needs acid — don’t raise the pH right before it.
discriminator: Aluminum in sucralfate accumulates in CKD.

A.text: It needs acid to polymerize and bind the ulcer base
A.why: Sucralfate polymerizes in acid (pH below 4) to form a protective barrier over the ulcer base; separate it from other drugs by 2 hours.

C.text: It irreversibly blocks the proton pump

stem: A patient with confirmed H. pylori took azithromycin for bronchitis 2 months ago and has no drug allergies. Which regimen is preferred?
why_correct: Recent macrolide exposure raises clarithromycin-resistance concern, so bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI + bismuth + metronidazole + tetracycline) is preferred.
takeaway: Macrolide history, clarithromycin resistance, or penicillin allergy → bismuth quadruple.
discriminator: Penicillin allergy alone in triple therapy: metronidazole replaces amoxicillin.

C.why: Recent macrolide exposure raises clarithromycin-resistance concern, so bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI + bismuth + metronidazole + tetracycline) is preferred.

stem: A 70-year-old has taken omeprazole for 8 years. Which complication is a class-wide long-term risk?
why_correct: Long-term PPIs: B12 deficiency, hypomagnesemia, fractures, C. difficile, pneumonia, interstitial nephritis; rebound acid on stopping.
takeaway: Reassess long-term PPIs periodically.
discriminator: Gynecomastia = cimetidine; tardive dyskinesia = metoclopramide.

E.why: Long-term PPIs: B12 deficiency, hypomagnesemia, fractures, C. difficile, pneumonia, interstitial nephritis; rebound acid on stopping.

stem: A patient beginning highly emetogenic chemotherapy needs prevention. Which regimen follows the taught principle?
why_correct: Combine classes with different targets (5-HT3, NK1, dexamethasone); avoid duplicating one mechanism.
takeaway: Stack different mechanisms, not more of one.
discriminator: Textbook: the triple combination prevents acute emesis in 80–90%.

D.why: Combine classes with different targets (5-HT3, NK1, dexamethasone); avoid duplicating one mechanism.

stem: Why do PPIs suppress acid more completely than H2 receptor antagonists?
correct: They block the pump, the final common pathway

distractors.text: They block both histamine and gastrin receptors
distractors.why: PPIs act at the pump, not receptors.

distractors.text: They neutralize acid already in the stomach
They act faster than any other class

why_correct: Gastrin, histamine and acetylcholine converge on the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase; PPIs block it irreversibly, so suppression occurs whatever the input.
takeaway: Block the last step and every input is silenced.
discriminator: H2 blocker = one input (histamine); PPI = the pump itself.

A.text: They neutralize acid already in the stomach

B.text: They act faster than any other class

C.text: They block both histamine and gastrin receptors
C.why: PPIs act at the pump, not receptors.

D.text: They block the pump, the final common pathway
D.why: Gastrin, histamine and acetylcholine converge on the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase; PPIs block it irreversibly, so suppression occurs whatever the input.

stem: Before starting azathioprine for Crohn maintenance, which test is most important?
why_correct: Test TPMT and NUDT15 before thiopurines; low activity raises myelosuppression risk.
takeaway: Thiopurines: gene-test first, then CBC and LFTs.
discriminator: Allopurinol cuts thiopurine breakdown — reduce dose by about two-thirds to three-quarters.

C.why: Test TPMT and NUDT15 before thiopurines; low activity raises myelosuppression risk.

stem: A patient on apixaban asks about ginkgo for memory. What is the key concern?
why_correct: Ginkgo (and fish oil) can increase bleeding risk, especially with anticoagulants/antiplatelets; stop before surgery.
takeaway: Bleeding supplements: ginkgo, fish oil (textbook adds garlic, ginseng).
discriminator: St. John’s wort lowers drug levels; ginkgo adds bleeding.

A.why: Ginkgo (and fish oil) can increase bleeding risk, especially with anticoagulants/antiplatelets; stop before surgery.

stem: A patient on bismuth quadruple therapy calls about black stools and plans to drink beer this weekend. What is the most important counseling?
correct: Black stool is expected; avoid alcohol with metronidazole

distractors.text: Stop all therapy — black stool means bleeding
Alcohol is fine; only tetracycline interacts
Take tetracycline with milk to protect the stomach
Double the PPI to stop the black stool

why_correct: Bismuth causes harmless black stool and tongue; metronidazole plus alcohol causes a disulfiram-like reaction (avoid during and 3 days after).
takeaway: Metronidazole: no alcohol. Tetracycline: no dairy, antacids, iron.
discriminator: Bismuth black stool can mimic GI bleeding — counsel ahead.

A.text: Double the PPI to stop the black stool

B.text: Alcohol is fine; only tetracycline interacts

C.text: Stop all therapy — black stool means bleeding

D.text: Take tetracycline with milk to protect the stomach

E.text: Black stool is expected; avoid alcohol with metronidazole
E.why: Bismuth causes harmless black stool and tongue; metronidazole plus alcohol causes a disulfiram-like reaction (avoid during and 3 days after).

stem: A patient on warfarin and phenytoin starts an H2 blocker. Which choice raises both drug levels?
why_correct: Cimetidine is a potent CYP450 inhibitor (1A2, 2C19, 3A4) that raises warfarin, phenytoin, and theophylline levels.
takeaway: Cimetidine = CYP inhibitor + antiandrogenic.
discriminator: Antacids/sucralfate bind drugs in the gut; cimetidine inhibits liver enzymes.

B.why: Cimetidine is a potent CYP450 inhibitor (1A2, 2C19, 3A4) that raises warfarin, phenytoin, and theophylline levels.

stem: Two weeks after finishing H. pylori therapy, a patient still on a PPI asks for a breath test. What is the best plan?
correct: Wait ≥ 4 weeks after therapy, PPI held 2 weeks

distractors.text: Test now while still on the PPI
Skip testing if symptoms are gone
Test only if an ulcer bleeds again

why_correct: Confirm eradication at least 4 weeks after therapy with the PPI held for 2 weeks to avoid false negatives.
takeaway: Test of cure: wait 4 weeks, hold the PPI 2 weeks.
discriminator: Urea breath test or stool antigen.

A.text: Wait ≥ 4 weeks after therapy, PPI held 2 weeks
A.why: Confirm eradication at least 4 weeks after therapy with the PPI held for 2 weeks to avoid false negatives.

B.text: Test now while still on the PPI

C.text: Test only if an ulcer bleeds again

E.text: Skip testing if symptoms are gone

stem: A patient takes very large doses of loperamide to get high. What toxicity is the main concern?
why_correct: Very high loperamide doses cause QT prolongation, torsades and cardiac arrest; naloxone reverses CNS depression.
takeaway: Loperamide: safe at normal doses, cardiotoxic at abuse doses.
discriminator: P-gp normally keeps it out of the CNS.

A.why: Very high loperamide doses cause QT prolongation, torsades and cardiac arrest; naloxone reverses CNS depression.

stem: Which IBD agent is most gut-selective?
why_correct: Vedolizumab blocks α4β7 integrin-mediated leukocyte gut-homing — less systemic immunosuppression.
takeaway: α4β7 = the gut’s address tag.
discriminator: -zumab humanized (vedolizumab); -ximab chimeric (infliximab).

E.why: Vedolizumab blocks α4β7 integrin-mediated leukocyte gut-homing — less systemic immunosuppression.

stem: Which vitamins carry the greatest accumulation and toxicity risk?
why_correct: Fat-soluble vitamins are stored in fat and liver and accumulate; water-soluble vitamins are renally excreted and rarely toxic.
takeaway: ADEK stay; B and C wash away.
discriminator: Vitamin D toxicity: hypercalcemia, kidney stones.

D.why: Fat-soluble vitamins are stored in fat and liver and accumulate; water-soluble vitamins are renally excreted and rarely toxic.

stem: Which factor tips the mucosal balance toward injury by removing prostaglandin protection?
why_correct: NSAIDs block COX-1 prostaglandins that drive mucus, bicarbonate and mucosal blood flow, tipping the balance toward aggression.
takeaway: Aggressive: acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs. Protective: mucus–bicarbonate, prostaglandins, epithelial turnover.
discriminator: NSAIDs remove a defense; H. pylori adds an attack (urease → ammonia).

B.why: NSAIDs block COX-1 prostaglandins that drive mucus, bicarbonate and mucosal blood flow, tipping the balance toward aggression.

stem: A Crohn patient on azathioprine is prescribed allopurinol for gout. What must happen?

distractors.text: Switch to febuxostat with no change

distractors.why: Dose reduction is the taught answer.

why_correct: Allopurinol blocks thiopurine metabolism; reduce the thiopurine dose by about two-thirds to three-quarters (febuxostat avoided).
takeaway: Allopurinol + thiopurine → big dose cut.
discriminator: Same interaction appears in Unit 2 (gout).

A.text: Switch to febuxostat with no change

B.why: Dose reduction is the taught answer.

D.why: Allopurinol blocks thiopurine metabolism; reduce the thiopurine dose by about two-thirds to three-quarters (febuxostat avoided).

stem: Which receptor does ondansetron block?
why_correct: Ondansetron blocks serotonin 5-HT3 receptors on gut vagal afferents and the CTZ.
takeaway: -setron = 5-HT3; -pitant = NK1; -izine = H1.
discriminator: Chemo/gut triggers → 5-HT3; motion → H1/M1.

C.why: Ondansetron blocks serotonin 5-HT3 receptors on gut vagal afferents and the CTZ.

stem: A severely malnourished patient with a functional gut needs nutrition. What is the best plan?
correct: Slow enteral feeding, thiamine first, daily electrolytes

distractors.why: If the gut works, use it.

why_correct: Use the gut if it works; refeed slowly, give thiamine before feeding, and check phosphate, potassium and magnesium daily at the start.
takeaway: If the gut works, use it — slowly.
discriminator: Refeeding: insulin drives phosphate, potassium, magnesium into cells.

D.why: If the gut works, use it.

E.text: Slow enteral feeding, thiamine first, daily electrolytes
E.why: Use the gut if it works; refeed slowly, give thiamine before feeding, and check phosphate, potassium and magnesium daily at the start.
